front: Toddler with ear pain and fever: which otoscopic findings diagnose acute otitis media, and how does otitis externa differ?
bottom: Moderate-severe tympanic membrane bulging or new otorrhea: acute otitis media.

bullets.clue: Otitis externa: tragus or pinna tenderness.
bullets.treat: Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day divided BID; amox-clav if amoxicillin within 30 days.
bullets.trap: Otitis externa: topical drops, not oral antibiotics.

back: Moderate-severe tympanic membrane bulging or new otorrhea: acute otitis media. Key clue: Otitis externa: tragus or pinna tenderness. First-line: Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day divided BID; amox-clav if amoxicillin within 30 days. Exam trap: Otitis externa: topical drops, not oral antibiotics.

diagram.alt: Acute otitis media: bulging tympanic membrane, high-dose amoxicillin; otitis externa treated with topical drops.

source.guideline: AAP Acute Otitis Media Guideline (2013); AAO-HNSF Acute Otitis Externa Guideline (2014)
source.recommendation: AAP 2013 KAS 1A/1B diagnosis by bulging TM or new otorrhea; KAS 4A amoxicillin, 4B β-lactamase coverage if amoxicillin in 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis or recurrent AOM; AAP dosing table 80–90 mg/kg/day BID; observation option for nonsevere ≥24 months. AAO-HNSF 2014: no systemic antimicrobials initially for uncomplicated AOE.

front: Sore throat, fever, no cough, tonsillar exudate: how to test and treat? And when do adults with sinusitis get antibiotics?
bottom: Test for strep; treat positives with penicillin or amoxicillin.

bullets.clue: Child with negative rapid test: back-up culture.
bullets.treat: Penicillin or amoxicillin 10 days; sinusitis: amoxicillin ± clavulanate 5–10 days.
bullets.trap: Adults don't need back-up culture; sinusitis may get watchful waiting.

back: Test for strep; treat positives with penicillin or amoxicillin. Key clue: Child with negative rapid test: back-up culture. First-line: Penicillin or amoxicillin 10 days; sinusitis: amoxicillin ± clavulanate 5–10 days. Exam trap: Adults don't need back-up culture; sinusitis may get watchful waiting.

diagram.alt: Strep pharyngitis: rapid test with culture back-up in children, penicillin or amoxicillin 10 days; adult sinusitis watchful waiting or amoxicillin.

source.guideline: IDSA Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis (2012); AAO-HNSF Adult Sinusitis Update (2015)
source.recommendation: IDSA: back up negative RADT with culture in children/adolescents, not routinely in adults; no testing with clear viral features; penicillin or amoxicillin usually 10 days. AAO-HNSF: watchful waiting or antibiotics for uncomplicated ABRS; amoxicillin ± clavulanate 5–10 days.

front: Active anterior nosebleed: first step, and when is packing used?
bottom: Firm sustained compression of the lower nose ≥5 minutes.

bullets.treat: Compression; then packing if bleeding persists.
bullets.trap: Anticoagulated or bleeding disorder: resorbable packing.

back: Firm sustained compression of the lower nose ≥5 minutes. Key clue: Most bleeding is anterior. First-line: Compression; then packing if bleeding persists. Exam trap: Anticoagulated or bleeding disorder: resorbable packing.

diagram.alt: Epistaxis: firm compression of the lower nose for at least 5 minutes, then packing, resorbable if on anticoagulants.

source.recommendation: AAO-HNSF 2020: firm sustained compression to the lower third of the nose ≥5 minutes; nasal packing if bleeding persists; resorbable packing with increased bleeding risk (anticoagulants/antiplatelets, bleeding disorders).

front: Sudden painless monocular vision loss: which fundus finding identifies central retinal artery occlusion, and what is the next step?
bottom: Pale retina with a cherry-red macula: central retinal artery occlusion.

bullets.treat: Immediate referral to stroke center or ED.
bullets.trap: Flashes, floaters or curtain: urgent dilated retinal exam for detachment.

back: Pale retina with a cherry-red macula: central retinal artery occlusion. Key clue: Painless, sudden, one eye. First-line: Immediate referral to stroke center or ED. Exam trap: Flashes, floaters or curtain: urgent dilated retinal exam for detachment.

diagram.alt: Central retinal artery occlusion: cherry-red spot, immediate stroke-center referral, giant cell arteritis workup over 50.

source.guideline: AAO PPPs: Retinal and Ophthalmic Artery Occlusions; Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Breaks and Lattice Degeneration
source.recommendation: AAO PPP: acute symptomatic CRAO/BRAO/OAO is an emergency; immediate referral to nearest stroke center/ED; systemic stroke evaluation; suspect GCA over 50 with urgent corticosteroids. AAO PVD/retinal breaks PPP: symptoms cannot distinguish PVD with or without a break, so a peripheral retinal exam (indirect ophthalmoscopy, scleral depression) is required; symptomatic patients need urgent ophthalmology evaluation.

front: Red eye with watery discharge after a cold: treatment, and what to avoid?

bullets.clue: Watery discharge, preauricular node, recent URI.
bullets.trap: Avoid indiscriminate topical antibiotics and steroids.

back: Viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis: supportive care. Key clue: Watery discharge, preauricular node, recent URI. First-line: Cool compresses, artificial tears, hygiene. Exam trap: Avoid indiscriminate topical antibiotics and steroids.

diagram.alt: Viral conjunctivitis: supportive care; avoid routine antibiotic or steroid drops.

source.recommendation: AAO PPP: avoid indiscriminate topical antibiotics or corticosteroids; viral conjunctivitis does not respond to antibacterials; mild bacterial conjunctivitis likely self-limited; no topical antibiotic superior.

front: Sudden one-sided hearing loss over 2 days, Weber lateralizes to the good ear: next steps?
bottom: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: urgent audiometry.

bullets.clue: Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear.
bullets.treat: Audiogram within 14 days; offer corticosteroids within 2 weeks.
bullets.trap: No routine head CT; MRI or ABR for retrocochlear lesion.

back: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: urgent audiometry. Key clue: Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear. First-line: Audiogram within 14 days; offer corticosteroids within 2 weeks. Exam trap: No routine head CT; MRI or ABR for retrocochlear lesion.

diagram.alt: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: audiometry within 14 days, corticosteroids within 2 weeks, MRI for retrocochlear lesion.

source.guideline: AAO-HNSF Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update 2019)
source.recommendation: AAO-HNSF 2019: audiometry as soon as possible (≤14 days); no routine CT; MRI or ABR for retrocochlear pathology; may offer corticosteroids within 2 weeks; intratympanic steroid salvage 2–6 weeks. Vertigo/BPPV: see pance-105 (neuro).

front: When do people with diabetes need retinal screening, and what treats center-involved macular edema?
bottom: Dilated eye exam: type 2 at diagnosis, type 1 within 5 years.

bullets.clue: Normal exams and controlled glucose: every 1–2 years.
bullets.treat: Center-involved DME with vision loss: intravitreal anti-VEGF.
bullets.trap: Any retinopathy: at least yearly exams.

back: Dilated eye exam: type 2 at diagnosis, type 1 within 5 years. Key clue: Normal exams and controlled glucose: every 1–2 years. First-line: Center-involved DME with vision loss: intravitreal anti-VEGF. Exam trap: Any retinopathy: at least yearly exams.

diagram.alt: Diabetic retinopathy screening at diagnosis for type 2 and within 5 years for type 1; anti-VEGF for center-involved macular edema.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 section 12; AAO Diabetic Retinopathy PPP (2024)
source.recommendation: ADA 2026: dilated exam at T2 diagnosis and within 5 years of T1 onset; every 1–2 years if normal and glycemia at goal; at least annually with retinopathy. AAO PPP: anti-VEGF effective for center-involved DME with vision loss.

front: Elevated eye pressure with optic disc cupping: first-line drug? And first-line for wet macular degeneration?

bullets.treat: Prostaglandin analog drops; wet AMD: intravitreal anti-VEGF.
bullets.trap: AREDS2 vitamins only for intermediate or one-eye advanced AMD.

back: Open-angle glaucoma: prostaglandin analog first. Key clue: Painless peripheral vision loss, cupping. First-line: Prostaglandin analog drops; wet AMD: intravitreal anti-VEGF. Exam trap: AREDS2 vitamins only for intermediate or one-eye advanced AMD.

diagram.alt: Open-angle glaucoma treated first with prostaglandin analog drops; wet macular degeneration with anti-VEGF injections.

source.guideline: AOA Evidence-Based Guideline: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (2024); AAO Age-Related Macular Degeneration PPP (2024)
source.recommendation: AOA 2024: prostaglandin analogs strong initial option unless contraindicated. AAO 2024 AMD PPP: intravitreal anti-VEGF first-line for neovascular AMD; AREDS2 for intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in one eye.

front: Child with recurrent sore throats: when is tonsillectomy indicated?
bottom: Paradise criteria: 7 in 1 year, 5/year for 2, or 3/year for 3.

bullets.clue: Each episode documented with qualifying findings.
bullets.trap: Peritonsillar abscess: drain plus antibiotics; epiglottitis: secure airway first.

back: Paradise criteria: 7 in 1 year, 5/year for 2, or 3/year for 3. Key clue: Each episode documented with qualifying findings. First-line: Below threshold: watchful waiting. Exam trap: Peritonsillar abscess: drain plus antibiotics; epiglottitis: secure airway first.

diagram.alt: Tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection: 7 episodes in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years.

source.guideline: AAO-HNSF Tonsillectomy in Children (Update 2019); AAFP Peritonsillar Abscess review (2017); Acute epiglottitis review, PMC (2012)
source.recommendation: AAO-HNSF 2019: watchful waiting for recurrent throat infection unless ≥7 episodes in past year, ≥5/year for 2 years or ≥3/year for 3 years with documented qualifying findings. AAFP 2017: drain peritonsillar abscess by needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics. Epiglottitis review (PMC3498669): airway emergency; no imaging in respiratory distress; intubate in OR with spontaneous ventilation and tracheotomy backup.

front: Penetrating eye injury with a peaked pupil: first steps?
bottom: Suspected open globe: rigid shield, no pressure.

bullets.clue: Peaked pupil, extruded contents, low pressure.
bullets.treat: Shield, NPO, antiemetics, IV antibiotics, tetanus, urgent ophthalmology.
bullets.trap: No pressure or IOP check; CT, not MRI, for metal.

back: Suspected open globe: rigid shield, no pressure. Key clue: Peaked pupil, extruded contents, low pressure. First-line: Shield, NPO, antiemetics, IV antibiotics, tetanus, urgent ophthalmology. Exam trap: No pressure or IOP check; CT, not MRI, for metal.

diagram.alt: Open globe: rigid shield without pressure, antiemetics, antibiotics, CT orbits, urgent ophthalmology.

source.guideline: AAO EyeWiki: Pre-Ophthalmologist Management of Eye Trauma; Ruptured Globe; Hyphema
source.recommendation: AAO EyeWiki: rigid shield on orbital bone, no pressure or manipulation; NPO, analgesia, antiemetics, antibiotics, tetanus; noncontrast thin-slice CT, avoid MRI if metal possible; urgent repair. Hyphema: shield, head elevation, screen sickle status.
